steps.prompt: Choosing a president, vice-president and treasurer from $7$ people gives $210$ ways. How many ways are there to choose just a committee of $3$ from the same $7$? Why is it fewer?

cards.title: Choosing a group
cards.body: The number of ways to choose $k$ things from $n$ when order doesn't matter is $\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k! \, (n - k)!}$, read "$n$ choose $k$". It is the ordered count divided by $k!$, because each group can be ordered in $k!$ ways. Also $\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n - k}$.

cards.title: Worked example: a committee
cards.problem: How many committees of $3$ can be chosen from $7$ people?

steps.text: Each committee was counted $3! = 6$ times, so there are $\frac{210}{6} = 35$ committees.

cards.title: Paths, handshakes and lines
cards.body: A path on a grid that goes $a$ steps right and $b$ steps up is a string of $a + b$ moves; choose which $a$ of them go right: $\binom{a + b}{a}$ paths. $n$ people shaking hands once each: $\binom{n}{2}$. Lines through $n$ points with no three in a line: also $\binom{n}{2}$.

cards.title: Worked example: grid paths
cards.problem: How many shortest paths go from $(0, 0)$ to $(4, 3)$, moving one unit right or up at a time?

steps.text: Every path uses $4$ rights and $3$ ups: $7$ moves.

try.prompt: How many moves does each path have?

steps.text: Choose which $3$ of the $7$ moves are ups: $\binom{7}{3} = 35$ paths.

cards.title: The common trap: counting groups in order
cards.body: A committee, a hand of cards or a set of toppings has no order: divide the ordered count by $k!$. When a choice has two parts (two boys AND two girls), multiply the two combinations. When one person must be included, choose the rest from the others.

prompts: Give one example where order matters and one where it doesn't.
